title: Just Because Drill and Kill Rhyme
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that the slogan 'drill and kill' has persuaded teachers that repetitive practice inherently destroys motivation, and suggests its rhyme may be part of why, citing research that rhyming statements are judged more true. He defines a drill as repetitive practice intelligently designed and carried out to produce a learning result, and notes that athletes, musicians and deliberate-practice researchers like Ericsson rely on exactly this. Rather than a blanket rule, he returns to his five key beliefs of student motivation: credibility, value, belonging, effort and efficacy. Because success feeds all five, and repetition is the fastest route to success for things like vocabulary or mechanics, well-run drill can support motivation. He proposes a more accurate phrase: in some learning cases, drills work best.
points: Defining drill as intelligently designed repetitive practice separates it from busywork and worksheet-dumping.
The rhyme effect may explain why a catchy slogan has outlived evidence in education.
Motivation rests on five beliefs, and success, which drill can produce, strengthens all of them.
Deliberate practice is standard in expertise research and sport but treated as heretical in education.
quotes: I’m not an athletic coach of any kind, but I’ve read enough of them to know that human motivation isn’t murdered by drills. Look at world-class, well-motivated athletes or musicians, and you’ll find that even at their level a good deal of drilling fills their lives.

When statements rhymed (e.g., “What sobriety conceals, alcohol reveals”), participants were more likely to judge them as true than when the same statements didn’t (e.g., “What sobriety conceals, alcohol unmasks”).
When these beliefs are in place, a learner will want to learn and a learner will even happily engage (!) in drill work.
This is not chucking worksheets at kids, this is not ruling a room with an iron fist while kids do tons of busywork.

It’s crazy how chock-full the literature outside of education is with this idea — it’s called “deliberate practice” by expertise researchers like K. Anders Ericsson — and how heretical it is inside of education.

One of the few paths that all five of these beliefs have in common is success. When our students succeed in our classes, especially at things that are difficult, they’re more likely to think that we’re good teachers, that the work matters, that their identities align with the work, that their effort matters, and that they’ll succeed again.
